Coushatta

Coushatta histories connect distinct communities in Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma. This reading path distinguishes the peoples and their governments while introducing community history, archives and public language work.

Names & relationshipsSome sources use “Koasati” for the language associated with Coushatta communities; here, “Coushatta” names the people/community collection and “Koasati” primarily names the language. Neither label is a synonym for Alabama. The Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas and Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town in Oklahoma are distinct governments and communities. Their connections do not make every family’s route, language use or political history identical. A joint Texas government is not evidence that Alabama and Coushatta were originally one people. The 1987 federal act and the Texas Tribe’s constitution describe one joint legal/governmental status for the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas while also recognizing that Alabama and Coushatta were formerly distinct peoples; this legal arrangement does not make the three present governments interchangeable.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
Adequate initial introduction

Thirteen substantive inspected works now include distinct Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma community perspectives; community historical and language materials; the Louisiana Tribe’s public Koasati digital dictionary; federal legal texts; and dated scholarship. Together they support a bounded educational introduction while keeping the Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma governments distinct. The language dictionary was sampled through four entries, and the source count does not establish completion, exhaustive coverage, endorsement or current legal advice.

Assessment recorded October 23, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • The Texas statute’s contemplated proclamation and its implementation record were not inspected; later legal interpretation remains outside scope.
  • The treaty is an edited transcription; manuscript, ratification record and Indigenous responses were not examined here.
  • The 1932 secondary article is dated and draws on older terminology and sources; further Coushatta-authored history and direct archival research would improve the account.
  • The digital dictionary was sampled through four entries; full vocabulary coverage, grammar, additional teaching materials and present-day language context remain open.
  • Current community conditions and each Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma government’s own contemporary publications require further review; no present census or language-use estimate is claimed.
  • No community review or endorsement has been recorded.

01

The shared Texas government has a particular history

The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas describes Alabama and Coushatta as separate peoples with a long association. Its history connects migration into East Texas with relationships under successive colonial and state governments. The Tribe’s timeline dates federal restoration to 1987. This public account concerns the joint Texas institution, rather than making Louisiana and Oklahoma Coushatta communities branches of that government.

Read the sources [1] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas

02

Village leaders and a changing institutional name

The Tribe’s Chief History distinguishes leaders of Alabama villages, leaders of Coushatta villages and later Alabama-Coushatta chiefs. It names Coushatta leaders associated with different Texas communities and describes movement onto the Alabama reservation beginning in 1859. The publication’s structure makes village-level histories visible; it should not be read as proof that every earlier Coushatta community belonged to one unchanged modern government.

Read the sources [2] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas

03

The treaty text records a proposal, not a settled outcome

An edited transcript of the February 23, 1836 treaty names Alabama and Coushatta among groups styled “associate Bands” of the Cherokee, then proposes that those groups form one community within a described area. The document records a Republic of Texas negotiating position in that moment. Later historical accounts report that the agreement was not ratified; its text alone does not establish implementation, Indigenous acceptance of the proposed terms, or a continuing boundary.

Read the sources [12] Texas History Trust, Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest [14] Texas Historical Commission

04

Federal law changed the Texas government’s legal relationship

The 1954 federal statute provided for transfer of trust lands to Texas and termination of federal supervision and services following a proclamation. In 1987, Congress restored federal recognition, the trust relationship and services for the Alabama and Coushatta Tribes of Texas, treating them as one tribal unit for federal-law purposes. The Tribe’s constitution, amended through 2023, says the Alabama and Coushatta were formerly distinct tribes and describes their shared legal government, territory and governing institutions. These legal texts concern the Texas government; they do not erase separate peoplehood or describe other Coushatta governments.

Read the sources [10] United States Congress; Statutes at Large, vol. 68, pp. 768–769 [11] United States Congress; Statutes at Large, vol. 101, pp. 666–673 [9] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas

05

A 1932 history is useful only with its period and viewpoint visible

Harriet Smither’s long article follows Alabama history in Texas through colonial records, nineteenth-century land negotiations and federal reports. It provides a route into dated records, including petitions and land actions, but its terminology and descriptions reflect an early twentieth-century outside historian. This page uses it selectively as a historical source and does not carry its old population statements or character judgments forward as current fact.

Read the sources [13] Southwestern Historical Quarterly, 36(2), October 1932, pp. 83–108; Texas State Historical Association

06

A state history article revisits the Texas Revolution story

The Texas Historical Commission’s 2026 article summarizes the Alabama-Coushatta role in events around the Texas Revolution, quoting historical sources and an attributed statement by Chief Colita. It also reports that the Texas Senate declined to ratify the 1836 treaty. Because this is a modern state-agency retrospective, its quotations and historical interpretations remain attributed to that article and its named sources.

Read the sources [14] Texas Historical Commission [12] Texas History Trust, Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest

07

An archive route still awaiting inspection

The original Coushatta tribal-archive link remains available as a reading route, but its body could not be retrieved in this pass. No underlying collection item, narrative, image, recording or access permission was reviewed through it.

Read the sources [7] Original directory route: Coushatta tribal archives, hosted at Washington State University

08

Louisiana’s account of movement and institutional renewal

The Louisiana Tribe’s history describes successive settlements across a changing colonial borderland and an enduring community near Elton. It attributes renewed federal recognition in 1973 to years of community organizing and advocacy after services were withdrawn. These are the Tribe’s institutional historical statements. Its trajectory differs from the Texas restoration chronology and does not establish current eligibility, services or every family’s migration.

Read the sources [3] Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana

09

Community decisions in language documentation

Bertney and Linda Langley describe a Koasati Language Committee whose members made spelling decisions and shaped practical teaching materials. Their account connects workshops, documentation training and collaborative review with community control of the resulting work. It records activities beginning in 2006–2007, rather than current program delivery. The chapter explains a process; its reported successes are not an independently measured learner-fluency outcome.

Read the sources [4] American Indian Language Development Institute, University of Arizona

10

Texas connections extend beyond present government locations

TxDOT’s April 2021 report explicitly acknowledges collaboration with the Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana’s heritage staff. It describes several Coushatta communities in Texas and related travel networks connecting Texas and Louisiana. The account treats village decisions and movements separately. This history helps explain why a Louisiana-based government can have Texas interests; it is not a new territorial boundary or a claim that everyone followed one route.

Read the sources [5] Texas Department of Transportation, Tribal Histories Project

11

The Oklahoma town’s own historical perspective

Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town describes Alabama and Quassarte as earlier distinct towns within the Muscogee Confederacy. Its history differentiates people who moved southwest into Louisiana and Texas from those removed with the Creeks to Indian Territory. The Oklahoma community’s continuing institutional story is therefore a separate reading path, rather than another name for the Texas or Louisiana government.

Read the sources [6] Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town

12

Community language work and a public Koasati dictionary

A community-coauthored AILDI chapter describes Koasati documentation workshops and the Language Committee’s decisions about writing and teaching materials. The Louisiana Coushatta Tribe’s public digital dictionary names its committee, guides and editor and provides word forms, definitions and selected examples. A separate short language page identifies Alabama as related to Koasati, not another name for it. Together these sources document Louisiana-centered language work; they do not establish identical practice across Texas and Oklahoma Coushatta institutions, a current speaker count, or measured learning outcomes.

Read the sources [8] Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana [4] American Indian Language Development Institute, University of Arizona [15] Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, McNeese State University, and the College of William & Mary

What needs further research

  • The public Koasati Digital Dictionary is now represented through its introduction and four selected entries. Review its full vocabulary and community teaching resources, and consult specialist Koasati grammar where accessible; do not infer current language vitality or learning outcomes from a partial dictionary sample.
  • Expand current Coushatta-authored historical and institutional accounts without treating Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma communities as interchangeable.
  • Inspect the 1954 proclamation, relevant state records and original treaty/ratification documents where accessible; keep statutory text distinct from later implementation.
  • Resolve contradictions in chief dates and organizational chronology through further evidence; do not silently choose whichever source sounds convenient.
  • Restore legitimate archive access if available later, with collection-level cultural permissions respected; no contact or restricted-material access attempted.
  • No present population, language vitality census, private genealogy or program outcome has been established.

The 1954 statute is cited as Public Law 83-627, 68 Stat. 768 (verified against the official Statutes at Large index); the 1987 restoration act is discussed only for Title II concerning the Texas Alabama-Coushatta Tribe. Constitution and By-Laws of the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas (amended through 2023) ↗

The Tribe’s own governing document describes the current legal name and says the Alabama and Coushatta were formerly distinct peoples but constitute one federally recognized tribe for legal and governmental purposes. Its preamble identifies self-government, language, arts, crafts and cultural preservation among its stated purposes. This is an authoritative text of the Texas Tribe’s own law, not a complete account of all Coushatta communities.

Inspection scope: Actual 25-page PDF, title/publication and amendment history, preamble and Articles I–V (printed pp. 3–8), and selected later amendment material through printed p. 23 read. The profile uses only the public name, organizational structure and stated purposes; detailed enrollment provisions and personal data are omitted. No independent legal opinion is offered.

Public Law 83-627: An Act to provide for the termination of Federal supervision over the property of the Alabama and Coushatta Tribes of Indians of Texas ↗

The enacted 1954 law describes conveyance of federally held trust lands to Texas to be held in trust for the Alabama and Coushatta Tribes, and provides for termination of the federal relationship and services following the proclamation specified in the act. The page header/OCR is inconsistent about the public-law number; the Statutes at Large front matter identifies the Alabama-Coushatta act at 68 Stat. 768 as Public Law 83-627, while Public Law 83-628 begins at p. 769. Citation follows the official index and page range. The law is not evidence that the people or Tribe ceased to exist.

Inspection scope: Both scanned pages, all operative sections 1–8 (68 Stat. 768–769), read from GovInfo. Effective language is tied to the proclamation named in the statute; the proclamation itself and state implementation were not inspected in this review.

GovernmentUnited States Congress; Statutes at Large, vol. 101, pp. 666–673Source 11

Public Law 100-89, Title II: Alabama and Coushatta Indian Tribes of Texas ↗

Title II of the 1987 restoration law treats the Alabama and Coushatta Tribes of Texas as one tribal unit for federal-law purposes, restores federal recognition and the trust relationship, and makes federal services available under the act. The joint legal status is not a claim that Alabama and Coushatta are one people or that other Coushatta communities share the Texas government.

Inspection scope: Actual 7-page Statutes at Large PDF; complete Title II, §§201–206, on printed pp. 669–673 read. Title I concerns Ysleta del Sur Pueblo and is not attributed to Coushatta. No later case law or current legal advice is claimed.

Treaty between Texas and the Cherokee Indians, February 23, 1836 (transcribed in Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, vol. I) ↗

The printed treaty text lists Alabama and Coushatta among groups it calls Cherokee “associate Bands” and proposes that the named bands form one community within specified bounds. This is a Republic of Texas diplomatic document in colonial/state language, mediated through a later edited transcription. Its text does not establish that the proposed agreement was ratified, implemented, or accepted as a lasting boundary by the named peoples. It is not a present homeland map.

Inspection scope: Transcript of the February 23, 1836 document on printed pages 14–15 of volume I reviewed through the Texas History Trust/University of North Texas text. The treaty’s opening and land-boundary article were inspected; the full volume, manuscript original, signatures and implementation record were not reviewed.

The Alabama Indians of Texas ↗

A substantial 1932 state-history article drawing on earlier colonial, Texas and federal records. Selected passages describe westward movement, Texas land petitions and reservation developments. The article uses period terminology, a dated outside scholarly frame and language that can be paternalistic; it is a source for what its author and cited records report, not a neutral or current community account. Historical population statements and characterizations are not reproduced as present facts.

Inspection scope: Selected actual pages of the 27-page PDF / printed pp. 83–108 inspected, including early migration, the 1850s land/reservation narrative and federal reports through the 1928 land purchase (PDF pp. 1–5, 13–16, 19, 25). The entire article and cited archival records were not independently checked. JSTOR terms appear in the scan; no reuse of its text or images is made.

Koasati Digital Dictionary — Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, with McNeese State University and William & Mary ↗

An open community digital dictionary whose landing page describes Koasati as a living language of the Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, explains its teaching and intergenerational purpose, and names its Language Committee, guides, editor and university partners. Four selected entries demonstrate listed word forms, definitions, English reversals and one example sentence. This is a Louisiana Coushatta language resource, not evidence that every Coushatta community shares identical current language practice; no speaker census or learning outcomes are claimed.

Inspection scope: Actual landing-page text read for the resource purpose, collaborators, full named Language Committee, guides and editor. Four actual entries inspected: aibachilka, ahoobalaho, chaihalaho and chinto palki. Reviewed their parts of speech, listed forms, English definitions/reversals and the one displayed example sentence. Full dictionary coverage, audio, linked materials and current use or learning outcomes were not assessed.
